shows.title: Dan Flavin: Grids
shows.description:
This is the first exhibition to focus specifically on Dan Flavin's grids, a body of fluorescent-light work he began in 1976 and returned to for years afterward. Flavin built these pieces from equal numbers of lamps facing forward and backward in a corner, so the sculpture throws contrasting color both out into the room and inward onto itself — a deceptively simple structure that turns out to be one of his most chromatically complex. David Zwirner has recreated several of Flavin's own historical installations rather than simply hanging the works flat on a wall, including a twenty-four-foot grid built from three museum loans and reunited here for the first time since a 1987 Castelli Gallery show honoring Leo Castelli's thirtieth anniversary as a dealer.

Among the highlights are Flavin's very first grids from 1976, a pair of pink-and-green constructions made for his Otis Art Institute show in Los Angeles and dedicated to that gallery's director and his wife, installed here exactly as they were then. Later works dedicated to Castelli show the artist loosening his palette into freer color combinations of yellow, blue, green and pink.

Having debuted in an expanded form at David Zwirner New York earlier in the year, the Hong Kong presentation is the first solo exhibition of Flavin's work anywhere in Greater China — a rare chance to see how thoroughly a commercial fluorescent tube, arranged with total rigor, can restructure the way a room feels.

venue.name: David Zwirner
venue.address: 80 Queen's Road Central, Central, Hong Kong

shows.title: Why the Butterflies
shows.description:
Nicole Wittenberg's first exhibition in Asia gathers a body of new paintings of coastlines, gardens, and flowers rendered at dusk — each canvas completed, by the artist's own method, in a single sitting and never reworked. The urgency of that process is the point: Wittenberg starts from plein-air pastel studies of a place before moving to canvas, trying to preserve the charge of a fleeting sensation rather than describe a scene. The results are big, loose, saturated fields of color that read as much as records of feeling as of place.

The pictures on view move between Maine's rocky coast, a friend's Paris apartment recalled from memory, and dusk in the mountains of Thailand, giving the show a loose travelogue structure even though nothing here is really about location. Some of the smaller works are painted with a wide broom-like brush more commonly used for her large-scale canvases, which forces an odd intimacy — a big gesture compressed into a small format. It's a neat trick that makes the modestly sized paintings feel just as physical as the room's largest works.

Wittenberg, a New York-based painter with pieces in the Guggenheim and the Boston MFA, has built a career out of pastel-to-canvas landscapes that lean on the Venetian school and American landscape painting as much as on Impressionism. This show, her first in Southeast Asia, was reportedly painted to a single Prince album on loop, and takes its title from the record's closing track — an odd, apt soundtrack for paintings that are all about holding onto a feeling before it passes.

venue.name: MASSIMODECARLO
venue.address: 10 Hollywood Road, Central, Hong Kong
venue.address_detail: Shop 03-205A & 205B & 206, Second Floor, Barrack Block, Tai Kwun

shows.title: At 25: Artists' Early Worlds, Part II
shows.artist: Salima Hashmi, Holly Lee, Bahc Yiso, Raqs Media Collective
shows.description:
This is the closing chapter of a two-part exhibition Asia Art Archive organized for its 25th anniversary, asking a deceptively simple question: what were these artists like at 25, the age when a practice is still finding its footing? Part II turns to Pakistani artist and educator Salima Hashmi, Hong Kong photographer Holly Lee, the late Korean artist Bahc Yiso, and the Delhi-based collective Raqs Media Collective, pairing rarely seen archival materials — student photographs, letters, early exhibition ephemera — with actual early works and a newly commissioned piece by Raqs Media Collective.

Rather than a conventional retrospective, the show works like an annotated scrapbook of formation: report cards of ambition before the polish of a mature style sets in. Seeing Holly Lee's early photographic experiments or the germs of Raqs's collective practice alongside the archival record around them gives a rare, unvarnished view of how an artistic voice gets built, shaped as much by teachers, politics, and circumstance as by talent.

Because AAA operates as a research library rather than a conventional white cube, the installation sits inside its working reading room on Hollywood Road, surrounded by the archive's own shelves — a fitting frame for a show fundamentally about how documentation shapes the stories we tell about artists. Free curator-led tours run through the run in both English and Cantonese, worth booking ahead since the space is intimate.

venue.name: Asia Art Archive
venue.address: 11/F, 233 Hollywood Road, Sheung Wan, Hong Kong

shows.title: The Pleasure-Dome of Hills: A Curated Hallucination of a Modern Literati
shows.artist: Chan Cho Kiu Bunchi, Emily Cheng, Dave Chow Yui Wang, Huang Dan, Ashlee Ip, Vann Kwok, Lam Duen Shan Ming, Lau Hiu Tung, Mindy Lui, Gerald Mak, Tse Chun Sing, Wengio Wong, Zhang Zhihui
shows.description:
Marking Ora-Ora's twentieth anniversary and its first collaboration with independent Hong Kong curator Zoie Yung, this group show stages a fictional scholar's studio inside the gallery's Tai Kwun home. Ming-dynasty huanghuali, Qing-dynasty zitan and Republican-era rosewood furniture — nodding to the antique trade once concentrated along Hollywood Road — sit alongside contemporary paintings, sculpture and wearable art by thirteen mostly Hong Kong-based artists.

The connecting thread is shanshui, or landscape, reimagined through the lens of urban walking and hiking, pastimes that define how Hong Kong residents relate to the hills ringing their city. Dave Chow's ink-toned canvas is pulled directly from the underside of a gym treadmill belt, translating the indoor "peaks" of daily exercise into abstract topography, while Vann Kwok's metalwork evokes skeletal mountain forms and Ashlee Ip's paintings chart rhythm and time through colour. New York-based Emily Cheng brings a more cosmological register, and ink painter Huang Dan strips landscape down to a spare, unadorned register.

Structured as a walk from Tai Kwun's furniture-lined streets up toward the hiking trails above, the exhibition asks what it means to look at land and the past through the filter of the present — a fitting question for a gallery marking two decades in this particular corner of Central.

venue.name: Galerie Ora-Ora
venue.address: 105-107, Barrack Block, Tai Kwun, 10 Hollywood Rd

shows.title: Tomorrow, the Tide Will Rise Again
shows.description:
itit Cheung's solo show at Videotage grows out of long stretches of time spent submerged in water, and it treats that bodily experience — the altered sense of breath, gravity, and duration underwater — as a way of thinking about grief and persistence. Rather than illustrating loss directly, the work builds an atmosphere in which the slow transformation of ordinary materials stands in for the way feelings change shape without disappearing: ice into water, one state of holding into another.

Cheung, who also works under the name Weera-it Ittiteerarak, has spent recent years working across video, sound, and installation with a recurring interest in tides, thresholds, and non-human rhythms; earlier pieces such as "I see พญานาค (Phaya Nāga) elsewhere" show the same pull toward liminal, half-submerged imagery. Here that language is distilled into a tighter body of new work built specifically around the push and pull of the tide as a metaphor for carrying what can't easily be put down.

It's a quiet, contemplative show rather than a spectacle-driven one, well suited to Videotage's long history of supporting new media and experimental practice in Hong Kong. Worth a visit for anyone interested in video and installation art that takes its time, and in an artist translating a very physical, personal experience of water into a shared meditation on holding on and letting go.

venue.name: Videotage
venue.address: Unit 13, Cattle Depot Artist Village, 63 Ma Tau Kok Road, To Kwa Wan, Kowloon, Hong Kong
hours: Mon - Fri 11:00am to 7:00pm (office hours, no exhibition)

shows.title: Collaboration in Collision
shows.artist: Fang Lijun, Kurt Chan Yuk-keung, Shiro Matsui, Raymond Fung Wing-kee, PRS, Juri Hwang, Andreas Kratky
shows.description:
This year's flagship exhibition turns the Arts Centre's own architecture into a participant rather than a backdrop, pairing four sets of artists — one Hong Kong, one visiting, in each case — across the atrium and the Pao Galleries. Curator Janet Fong frames the show around three ideas: the physical field of the building, the collision of creative approaches, and the collaboration that results, with the public invited to become a fifth kind of contributor.

The atrium centerpiece belongs to Chinese contemporary artist Fang Lijun, returning to the venue thirty-three years after his first Hong Kong showing here in 1993. His Ocean Ecology Series, made from recycled marine debris, is staged alongside a community-built installation assembled from plastic waste collected by local volunteers at a Big Wave Bay beach cleanup — a literal collision of established artist and public hand. Elsewhere, Hong Kong's Kurt Chan Yuk-keung and Japan's Shiro Matsui, working across ceramics, water and 3D printing, explore cosmological questions despite having barely met before the show; architect-painter Raymond Fung Wing-kee joins the multidisciplinary studio PRS for a three-part narrative spanning architecture, digital media and stage design; and the artist couple Juri Hwang and Andreas Kratky use technology and spatial perception to probe questions of belonging and displacement.

Structured as a single ascending path from the ground-floor atrium up into the galleries, the show leans hard into its premise that art here is made in dialogue with the building itself, continuing the Arts Centre's decade-plus run of flagship exhibitions built around cross-cultural, cross-disciplinary pairing.

venue.name: Hong Kong Arts Centre
venue.address: 2 Harbour Road, Wan Chai
venue.address_detail: Pao Galleries and Jockey Club Atrium

shows.title: Singing and Dancing with Brush and Ink: The Art of Wesley Tongson
shows.description:
This is the first major institutional survey of Hong Kong ink artist Wesley Tongson (1957–2012) since the early 2010s, bringing together close to thirty works on loan from M+, the Hong Kong Museum of Art, private collections and the Wesley Tongson Charitable Trust. Diagnosed with schizophrenia as a teenager, Tongson trained in traditional Chinese brushwork before spending decades pulling the medium apart: he developed a splash-ink method that fused Chinese landscape painting with gestural abandon, and by 2009 had given up the brush entirely, working ink into paper with his bare hands, fingers and fingernails.

The exhibition's five sections move chronologically through this evolution, from disciplined early studies grounded in classical technique to the raw, physically direct Spiritual Mountains series that closed his career. Curators Yi Yi Mon (Rosaline) Kyo and Julia M. White frame the work through the personal struggles that shaped it — Tongson's lifelong negotiation with mental illness, his fluid gender identity, and a spiritual practice that drew on Zen Buddhism, Taoism and Christianity all at once. Those threads surface not just in the paintings but in personal notes displayed alongside them.

Seeing early, rule-bound ink studies next to the late finger paintings makes the arc of Tongson's career legible in a way retrospectives rarely manage: this is an artist who didn't so much refine his technique over time as strip it down, piece by piece, until only the direct contact between hand and paper was left.

venue.name: Asia Society Hong Kong Center
venue.address: 9 Justice Drive, Admiralty, Hong Kong

shows.title: Lightness of Being
shows.description:
Curated by Leung Shiu Kee, Eric, this group show gathers eight young, mostly art-school-trained artists — several fresh out of Hong Kong Baptist University, the Chinese University of Hong Kong, and Hong Kong Art School — who all work from small, overlooked corners of daily life. The premise is unfussy: still lifes of household objects, charcoal drawings of a hometown, photographs of pedestrian gestures reworked into abstract paint, ceramic play-forms. It's the kind of show built to give a cohort of emerging local artists a first real wall to hang on.

A few threads stand out. Chau Sze Ling Aki's still lifes track the wear objects accumulate over time, while Tse Yuen Shan Angela pushes toward something more psychologically charged — her "Before Flushing" renders a bathroom faucet through a grieving figure's blurred, tearful vision. Leung Lok Yi Janice and On Tsz Tung both build invented, slightly anxious architectural spaces (breathing pores, emergency exits) rather than working from observation, giving the show a counterpoint between documentary tenderness and interior unease.

Nothing here is flashy, and that's rather the point — the show's title, borrowed loosely from the idea of dwelling in life's minutiae, describes its method as much as its mood. It's a useful snapshot of what's currently coming out of Hong Kong's art schools.

venue.name: Contemporary by Angela Li
venue.address: 248 Hollywood Road, Sheung Wan, Hong Kong

shows.title: Tranquil State: Eric Lai Wai Lam Solo Exhibition
shows.description:
Three years in the making, Tranquil State is Eric Lai Wai Lam's first solo show since 3812 Gallery began working with him through its YA! Young Art platform. Working in the meticulous gongbi technique, Lai builds paintings around a recurring cast of sparrows that have shifted over time from observed birds into stand-ins for the artist himself — figures that let him work through memory and emotion at one remove rather than painting himself directly.

Two of the anchor pieces, 11:11 and 22:22, take their titles and imagery from Cantopop lyrics by Wyman Wong (written for Joey Yung and Denise Ho), reworking the songs' fawns, rockets and falling angels into dense private codes layered over scenes from Lai's own life. Elsewhere, patterned tile floors, printed fabric and distant windows do more than set the scene — they thicken each picture into a lived-in space suspended between interior and exterior, memory and present tense.

It's a show built for slow looking: gongbi's demands for precision and the paintings' embedded ciphers reward the kind of patience the title promises, and the results are some of the most personal, quietly worked paintings in a program otherwise known for modern Chinese abstraction.

venue.name: 3812 Gallery
venue.address: 44 Wyndham Street, Central, Hong Kong

shows.title: City of Lights
shows.description:
British photographer Keith Macgregor spent the 1990s and 2000s methodically documenting Hong Kong's neon signage before it began disappearing under redevelopment, tightened signage regulation, and the switch to LED — and City of Lights pulls together a huge trove of that archive, much of it never previously exhibited. The pictures move through the city's after-dark geography: mahjong parlours in Wan Chai, nightclub marquees like Club Bboss in Tsim Sha Tsui, the crowded signage canyons of Nathan Road and Argyle Street, plus a few collaged, multi-exposure pieces that compress decades of the same street into a single frame.

What makes the work more than nostalgia is Macgregor's own reckoning with it — he's said he treated the signs as "urban wallpaper" for years before recognizing the craft behind them, and that shift in attention is the show's real subject. Seen together, the photographs double as a record of a specific, vanished trade: the glass-benders and installers who built these signs by hand, a handful of whom appear in the accompanying book he co-authored with heritage researcher Cardin Chan.

The exhibition coincides with the release of the City of Lights photobook from Blue Lotus Editions and arrives amid a broader wave of local interest in neon preservation, following recent surveys at the Hong Kong Design Institute and Tai Kwun. For anyone interested in Hong Kong's visual history, this is one of the most complete photographic accounts of that era currently on view.

venue.name: Blue Lotus Gallery
venue.address: 28 Pound Lane, Sheung Wan, Hong Kong

shows.title: FORM
shows.artist: Ailsa Wong, chaussette b., Gedvile Bunikyte, Jendrik Schröder, Joey Leung, Lie Fhung, Sin Sin Man
shows.description:
FORM brings together seven artists from Hong Kong, Indonesia, France, Lithuania and Germany who treat shape and material as processes rather than fixed outcomes. The range of media is wide — ceramics, ink and embroidery, geometric painting, photography, and assemblage — but the works share an interest in surfaces that record change: bark, skin, and roots standing in for the passage of time, or everyday materials reclaimed and reconfigured into something else entirely.

Ailsa Wong's paintings pull from automatic drawing and subconscious imagery to build inner landscapes; chaussette b. stitches ink and embroidery into textile studies of bark and memory; Gedvile Bunikyte's geometric canvases translate sacred-geometry motifs into luminous, meditative compositions. Jendrik Schröder's photographic "Leaf Studies" isolate fallen leaves as small exercises in ecological attention, while Joey Leung's interactive ceramic sculpture "The Form of the Good" invites viewers to physically participate in shaping the work, a nod to Plato. Lie Fhung assembles salvaged stained glass and oxidised copper into poetic fragments, and Sin Sin Man's "Determination" balances old hangers against stones in a precarious, quietly tense arrangement.

The gallery has also folded in three guest presentations — enamel jewellery, an indigenous-craft collection, and an ikebana-based floral installation — that push the show's inquiry into form beyond fine art into craft and material culture more broadly, making the case that "form" is a shared concern across very different practices and traditions.

venue.name: Sin Sin Fine Art
venue.address: Unit 4A, 26 Wong Chuk Hang Road, Aberdeen, Hong Kong

shows.title: Runway 51
shows.description:
American artist Barminski turns JPS Gallery's Staunton Street space into a full-scale cardboard airport terminal, complete with security checkpoint, departure lounge, gift shop and restroom, all rendered in his signature bold black outlines and flat colour. It's a follow-up to his 2023 show "Moon Lands On Man," and it keeps working the same vein of DIY sci-fi conspiracy: here the premise is that extraterrestrials aren't approaching from space but are already embedded in the mundane rituals of modern travel.

The installation unfolds as a sequence of stations rather than a conventional hang. Visitors pass through a checkpoint where a cardboard alien inspects a conveyor belt of Barminski's merchandise collaborations, browse a gift shop stocked with his hand-painted sculptures, and find a restroom whose mirrors reflect distant galaxies instead of the viewer's own face. A hidden door leads to a final room of video works tracing a fictional throughline of extraterrestrial influence from the pyramids to Stonehenge to Easter Island.

It's a maximalist, handmade environment more theme-park than gallery, and that's the point: Barminski trades in a scrappy, cardboard-and-spray-paint aesthetic that turns conspiracy theory into something closer to comic relief, undercutting cosmic dread with the banality of airport bureaucracy.

venue.name: JPS Gallery
venue.address: G/F, 88-90 Staunton Street, Central

shows.title: Reweaving Memory: Storytellers of Persia
shows.description:
Wei Gallery turns its Central space over to twenty antique Persian carpets spanning roughly 2,500 years, treating each one as a woven document rather than a decorative object. The pieces trace narrative and symbolic motifs — scenes drawn from the Shahnameh, royal hunting compositions, the Tree of Life, the mythical Simurgh and the Lion-and-Sun emblem — that carried Persian cultural memory through successive waves of conquest and dynastic change, from the Hellenistic and Islamic periods through the Safavids and beyond.

What makes the show worth lingering over is its argument about survival through use: these are carpets that were walked on, mended and handed down rather than sealed away, and the exhibition asks visitors to read their wear and repair as part of the content, not damage to look past. Seen together, the twenty examples function like chapters in a single long text, each pattern a fragment of language that outlived the empires that produced it.

It's a change of pace for a gallery better known for painting and sculpture, and a rare chance in Hong Kong to see this depth of historic Persian weaving in one room, spread across a run that stretches nearly a full year.

venue.name: Wei Gallery (Amanda Wei Gallery)
venue.address: 1 Chatham Path, Mid-Levels, Hong Kong

shows.title: The Feast of Joy (確幸)
shows.description:
Steven Tang paints the food of everyday Hong Kong — cold noodles, shrimp rice bowls, sandwiches, skewers — in coloured pencil and wood-colour drawings so exact they read as photographs from a few steps back. Up close, though, the hand is unmistakable: a self-taught, obsessive layering of pencil strokes that builds up grease, steam, and the particular sheen of a plastic lunchbox lid. The title, 確幸, borrows from the Chinese phrase for "small certain happiness" — the modest, reliable pleasures of a familiar meal.

Tang is entirely self-taught; he studied computer science at CUHK before starting his own studio, and his realist food pictures sold out at Art Central not long after he began showing publicly. That local, unpretentious subject matter is part of the appeal — these aren't luxury still lifes but the noodle shop and the cha chaan teng, rendered with a technical polish usually reserved for grander subjects.

This is Tang's fourth solo outing at Touch Gallery, following earlier "True to Form" shows built around the same premise: that realism, applied to the things people actually eat on a Tuesday, can carry as much feeling as any more obviously sentimental subject. The show rewards close looking — the pleasure is in spotting exactly how a strand of noodle or the condensation on a drink can was built up, stroke by stroke, in coloured pencil.

venue.name: Touch Gallery
venue.address: 10 Hollywood Road, Central, Hong Kong
venue.address_detail: Shop 103 & 202, 1-2/F, Block 3 Barrack Block, Tai Kwun

shows.title: A Shared Life in Time
shows.description:
A husband-and-wife pair of Japanese urushi (lacquer) artists show side by side at this Tai Kwun gallery devoted entirely to the medium. Hanako Gejo and Takeshi Igawa have spent parallel careers working the same slow, layered material — lacquer that must cure and be built up coat by coat — while pursuing distinct visual languages, and the exhibition is conceived as a portrait of a shared domestic and working life told through two independent bodies of work.

Gejo's pieces lean toward the ornamental and sculptural: vessels and forms enriched with shell inlay, gold leaf and metal powders, rendered with a fullness of volume she describes through her own vocabulary of restraint and richness. Igawa, by contrast, works in kanshitsu — dry lacquer built over a cloth-and-wood core — to produce sparer, more architectural forms that play black lacquer's density against its capacity to hold and reflect light; his sculptures "The Moon at Dusk" and "Migratory Bird II" typify this pared-back, almost geological sensibility.

Seen together, the two practices read less as a dialogue than as two instruments playing the same slow tune. It's a quiet, tactile show, well suited to a gallery whose entire mission is convincing Hong Kong audiences that lacquer belongs in the conversation about contemporary craft.

venue.name: The Gallery by SOIL
venue.address: Shop 102, 1/F, Barrack Block, Tai Kwun, 10 Hollywood Road

shows.title: Incising the Matrix: If Birdwood Block…
shows.description:
Jay Lau spent his residency at the Hong Kong Visual Arts Centre digging into the building's own past: Cassels Block, the Grade I structure that now houses the Centre, once had a twin, Birdwood Block, demolished decades ago and largely erased from memory. Lau treats that erasure as raw material, "incising" archival photographs of the old Victoria Barracks and running them through image-editing and AI tools to conjure alternate histories in which Birdwood Block never disappeared.

The result is a dispersed installation of prints and constructed images planted throughout the Centre's public stairwells and landings rather than confined to a single gallery room, so visitors encounter fabricated "documentary" scenes of a building that no longer exists (and, in this telling, perhaps never stopped existing) as they move through the real one. The images sit somewhere between architectural fantasy and forensic archive, deliberately blurring which parts are historical fact and which are speculative fabrication.

It's a sharp, site-specific way to use a residency: rather than importing outside work into the vA! building, Lau turns the building's own contested history into the subject, and the AI-assisted image-making becomes a tool for interrogating how photographic "evidence" gets constructed and trusted in the first place. Worth seeing as much for how it activates the Centre's unusual colonial-era architecture as for the images themselves.

venue.name: Hong Kong Visual Arts Centre (vA!)
venue.address: 7A Kennedy Road, Central, Hong Kong
venue.address_detail: Public Area on 1–5/F, inside Hong Kong Park

shows.title: 46 Sai Street
shows.description:
Xiao Bo names this show after Leo Gallery's own street address, using the site as a starting point for paintings built on his signature "Four Grids" method: each canvas divided into four equal sections that the artist works through in a repetitive, almost meditative bodily rhythm, with no preparatory sketch dictating the outcome. The imagery emerges from the process itself rather than being planned in advance — synchronized brushstrokes across the four panels that record small variations in the artist's movement rather than a picture of anything external.

The result is a body of abstract, grid-based paintings that read as records of duration and repetition more than as images — closer to a diary of physical labor than a window onto a scene. Following his 2025 solo show "Container" in Shanghai, this Hong Kong outing continues Xiao Bo's interest in painting as an "objective record of somatic breath," using the rigidity of the grid to strip away narrative and land on something closer to pure structure.

It's a rigorous, unshowy exhibition — worth seeing for how consistently Xiao Bo sustains a single formal idea across a full room of canvases, and for the way the show's title turns the gallery's own street number into part of the work's meaning.

venue.name: Leo Gallery
venue.address: 46 Sai Street, Sheung Wan, Hong Kong

shows.title: Revisiting the Jade Terrace: Exploring the Role of Female Ink Artists in Contemporary China
shows.artist: Chu Chu, Wang Mengsha, Zhang Yirong, Zhang Ying
shows.description:
This exhibition revisits a milestone in Alisan Fine Arts' history: in 2014 the gallery gave Chu Chu, Wang Mengsha and Zhang Yirong an early platform in the show "Beyond the Jade Terrace," a survey of the different ways contemporary women artists were reworking ink traditions. Twelve years on, the gallery brings the same three artists back together and adds a fourth, Zhang Ying, to see how their languages have matured. The result is less a retrospective than a status report: gongbi-trained figuration, photography stitched with calligraphy, and slow, spiritually inflected landscape painting sitting side by side.

Chu Chu's work fuses photographic imagery with brushed calligraphy, a hybrid practice that has landed her in museum collections from Philadelphia to the Centre Pompidou. Wang Mengsha has spent the past decade building a distinctive, widely recognized visual vocabulary through both gallery work and high-profile brand collaborations, while Zhang Yirong continues to refine an intensely careful gongbi technique that reanimates classical figure painting for a contemporary eye. Zhang Ying, the newer addition to this grouping, works in ink landscapes—rocks, trees, and mountains rendered with a meditative, almost devotional patience.

The show is staged as the "Now" half of a two-part, two-venue program tied to Alisan's 45th anniversary; a companion exhibition of four senior New Literati Movement painters runs concurrently at the gallery's Central space, framing a conversation across generations about where Chinese ink painting has been and where women artists are taking it next. Together the works trace a lineage from the 6th-century idea of the "Jade Terrace"—originally a cloistered space of women's writing—toward a more expansive contemporary studio practice.

venue.name: Alisan Atelier (Alisan Fine Arts)
venue.address: 1904 Hing Wai Centre, 7 Tin Wan Praya Road, Aberdeen, Hong Kong

shows.title: After Intelligence
shows.dates_note: Exact dates confirmed via the Hong Kong Art Gallery Association's live events calendar and Artomity magazine, since de Sarthe's own site is a JavaScript-only app that could not be rendered; the gallery's own page confirms the residency (deSAR) concluded Sept 4 and the resulting show opens Sept 5.
shows.description:
This show is the capstone of de Sarthe's ninth annual summer residency (deSAR), in which Hong Kong-born, New York-based artist Lau Wai spent two months using the gallery as an open studio, working in view of the public during normal hours. Lau's practice sits at the intersection of identity and emerging technology: they built a digital replica of themself, called W.A.I., using motion and facial capture, and have spent recent years investigating how CGI, data generation and virtual embodiment reshape the way identity is constructed and performed.

The resulting exhibition, After Intelligence, gathers the video, sculptural and installation work made during the residency, including pieces like The Cast of the Invisible, a single-channel CGI animation that treats the unseen labor behind digital doubles and performance-capture actors as its subject. It's a fitting continuation of Lau's longstanding interest — evident in earlier bodies of work built from 360-degree body scans and archival material — in how personal memory and virtual technology collide to produce new, unstable versions of the self.

Seeing the show fresh off a live studio residency gives it an unusual immediacy: these are very recent works, made in the same room where they're now installed, by an artist who has exhibited at institutions from Tai Kwun Contemporary to the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston.

venue.name: de Sarthe
venue.address: 2/F, Block A, Vita Tower, 29 Wong Chuk Hang Road, Wong Chuk Hang, Hong Kong

shows.title: Dazzled in the Loop
shows.description:
Cho Wing Ki paints Hong Kong's ordinary transit points — MTR escalators, roundabouts, footbridges — and turns them into fields of flattened, jewel-toned geometry. This solo show extends a body of work she's been developing for years, but pushes it further from documentary cityscape toward something more interior: less "here is a place" than "here is what it feels like to keep passing through it."

The strongest anchor pieces take specific, recognizable locations as their starting point. "The Escalating Whirl" reworks the long escalator at Admiralty MTR station into a dizzying study of reflection and ascent, while "Enchanting Cheung Wing" derives from the roundabout near the artist's own studio in Kwai Hing, its traffic and footbridges condensed into interlocking color blocks organized around an old banyan tree. Cho works primarily in oil but trained first as a printmaker (she is a member of the local collective Prinhow), and the show deliberately places prints next to paintings so viewers can see how repetition and layering — habits carried over from the printing process — get translated into her more recent painted surfaces.

The cumulative effect is a kind of urban rhythm-as-portrait: warm and cool tones stacked into tense, buoyant compositions that read as much as emotional states as depictions of place. It's a good entry point into a Hong Kong-trained painter (CUHK Fine Art, class of 2011) whose work sits at the more painterly, meditative end of the city's current crop of urban-landscape artists.

venue.name: Gallery EXIT
venue.address: 3/F, 25 Hing Wo Street, Tin Wan, Aberdeen, Hong Kong

shows.title: Isn't Love the Strangest Thing
shows.description:
Stanley Whitney's first solo exhibition in Asia takes its title from a 1936 Duke Ellington jazz standard about the disorienting mix of joy and sorrow that comes with falling in love — an apt reference for a painter who has spent decades building compositions out of loose grids of color that behave like musical phrases. Since the 1990s Whitney has organized his canvases into three or four bands of roughly rectangular fields, each one painted with a loose, visibly hand-worked edge, so that individual colors both hold their own ground and set up rhythms with their neighbors.

The paintings on view range from twelve to seventy-two inches square, giving a sense of how Whitney's color relationships shift with scale. His frequent references to jazz musicians like Charlie Parker and Ornette Coleman aren't incidental: the grid structure is his way of notating improvisation, with each block of color "calling" to the next much as a soloist responds to the rhythm section. The paintings also carry a debt to Black Southern quilting traditions and to the banded patterning of ancient Greek vase painting, linking Whitney's abstraction to lineages well outside the usual Ab-Ex reference points of Rothko or Gottlieb that his work is often measured against.

It's a tightly focused gallery show rather than a survey, but as an introduction to one of the most distinctive colorists working today, it's a strong one.

venue.name: Gagosian
venue.address: 12 Pedder Street, Central, Hong Kong

shows.title: A Strange Song Amongst the Snow
shows.description:
This group show, curated by Benchung, gathers thirteen young Tibetan artists — most showing outside Tibet for the first time — working across painting, textile, photography, and assemblage. Where an earlier generation of Tibetan contemporary artists responded to Lhasa's rapid modernization through recognizable iconography, this cohort works more obliquely, embedding meaning in materials pulled straight from daily and family life: yak wool braided with a mother's hair and siblings' umbilical cords, dried yak dung, sheep knucklebones, washing powder mailed from a home county, livestock-pen wood enclosing a cube of wool.

The works trade heavily in material memory rather than illustration. Karma Tsering's land-art assemblages and photographs address the fraying relationship between herders and the Qinghai-Tibet plateau; Tenzin Dhame's mineral-pigment paintings on Tibetan paper reinterpret founding myths to probe how the self "emerges from chaos"; Chakdor Kyab turns thirty-two collected caps and hats into a meditation on urban Tibetan identity. Younger artists here favor found and domestic objects over classical technique, even as their work stays rooted in Tibetan material culture.

Coming a year after Rossi & Rossi's "As The Wheel Turns," which surveyed the previous generation of established Tibetan artists, this exhibition functions as a generational counterpart — less a survey of a national style than a set of very personal reckonings with land, family, and the pressures of a rapidly urbanizing Tibet.

shows.title: TRACES: Yukihisa Isobe, Tetsuo Mizù
shows.description:
This two-person show puts two very different strands of postwar Japanese abstraction into direct dialogue for the first time. Yukihisa Isobe (b. 1935) made his name in the 1960s with the "Wappen" series — repeated heraldic-looking forms rendered in stone dust and embossed fresco textures — before stepping away from the studio for two decades to work as an ecological planner, later returning to art with land-art projects that map environmental change. Tetsuo Mizù (1944–2025), who died last year, spent his career translating international maritime signal flags into luminous geometric abstraction, encoding personal memory inside hard-edged color and form.

The pairing is built around a shared preoccupation: both artists devoted themselves to marking what risks disappearing, whether that's a vanishing ecology or a private history. Isobe's early board and canvas works from the late 1950s and early 1960s — thickly worked, materially rough — sit here against Mizù's cooler, more chromatic geometries, one practice forensic and cartographic, the other lyric and internal. Coming so soon after Mizù's passing, the show also plays as a quiet tribute, closing a six-decade arc between two artists who never showed together in life.

Visitors get a rare chance to see Isobe's rarely-exhibited early paintings and drawings from the Wappen period alongside a late-career survey of Mizù's flag-based abstractions — a compact but historically substantial pairing for anyone interested in the Gutai-adjacent generation of Japanese postwar art.

shows.title: Toil and Soil
shows.description:
Chiu Wei-Hsiang's paintings grow directly out of loss: raised in a rural Taiwanese township erased by a government airport-expansion project, the artist now works full-time in elder care, and both halves of that biography feed Toil and Soil. He paints from memory alone, without sketches or photographs, so contours blur and distort the way recollection does — a formal choice that doubles as subject matter, since the show is as much about the unreliability and ache of memory as about the rural world it depicts.

The paintings move between two kinds of labor that the art world rarely puts side by side: the physical, repetitive work of farming and market life that shaped Chiu's childhood, and the invisible, emotionally taxing labor of caring for the elderly and dying that shapes his present. Rather than treating his nursing-home subjects as clinical cases, he paints them with attention to their vitality, pushing back against the flattening logic of institutional care. A largely silent, observant child by his own account, Chiu treats painting itself as the language he didn't use out loud — pressure and color standing in for words.

It's a quietly political, deeply personal debut for the Hong Kong gallery from an artist worth watching, grounded in the particulars of one family's displacement but reaching well beyond it.

shows.title: Wayfarer of Fire
shows.artist: Brook Hsu, Kwan Sheung Chi, Lai Chih-Sheng, Phillip Lai, Ellen Pau, Apichatpong Weerasethakul, Samson Young
shows.description:
Taking its epigraph from Mallarmé, this group show gathers seven artists around the idea of fire as a transformative, communal and cinematic force — something tended, watched over and passed between hands rather than simply consumed. The throughline is cinema and its Promethean mythology: figures who keep the flame, who gather others around a story, who risk being burned by what they carry.

Ellen Pau's 1989–90 video "Blue," edited on Betamax to a Meredith Monk soundtrack, anchors the show with its oblique montage of war imagery and Hong Kong urban texture. Apichatpong Weerasethakul contributes "Of Love, Of Lights" and "Fireworks (Fans)," works that treat the bonfire as cinema's most primitive ancestor, while Phillip Lai's sculptural installations — a silent siren, a disorienting lighthouse beam set atop incinerated cereal — invert the theme into fire's uncanny absence. Brook Hsu's paintings riff on Pasolini, and Kwan Sheung Chi re-enacts the closing shot of Truffaut's "The 400 Blows."

It's a literate, image-heavy show built for close looking rather than spectacle, characteristic of this gallery's long-running interest in artists — several represented here for years — working through moving image, sound and quiet conceptual gesture rather than object-making for its own sake.

shows.title: The Lingering Departure
shows.description:
This is Tesfaye Urgessa's debut exhibition since joining White Cube in August 2026, and it lands in Hong Kong rather than London or New York — notable timing for an Ethiopian painter who represented his country at the Venice Biennale and has recently shown at Beijing's Red Brick Art Museum. Urgessa works in large-scale figuration, piling bodies together in tight, airless compositions that owe something to Freud's fleshiness and Bacon's distortions, filtered through a training that mixed Ethiopian art school fundamentals with Soviet-influenced anatomical rigor from his teachers and later study in Stuttgart.

The paintings and works on paper gathered here were made over the past year between Addis Ababa and Stuttgart, and take migration, family, and the strain of an unsettled political moment as their throughline. Urgessa has described his figures as caught in "a state of metamorphosis" — pressed against each other, merging with the rooms and objects around them, refusing to resolve into a single clean narrative. It's psychologically dense, sometimes uncomfortable painting, closer to reportage filtered through the body than to portraiture in any traditional sense.

For a gallery best known in Hong Kong for blue-chip Western names, betting its September slot on a recent signing making his Asia commercial debut is a real statement of intent, and worth seeing as much for what it signals about White Cube's direction as for the paintings themselves.
